planting.note: Set out container-grown stock in spring once frost risk has passed, sheltering young plants from drying wind until established.

directions: This Tasmanian rainforest endemic is the source of prized leatherwood honey and bears masses of large, white, four-petaled flowers with a central boss of stamens in mid to late summer. It needs cool, humid summers and consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, and resents both drought and waterlogging around its roots. Give it shelter from strong wind and hot afternoon sun, especially while young, and expect slow, steady growth into a dense, narrow evergreen tree or large shrub in favorable maritime climates. It is best suited to cool-summer coastal gardens rather than continental climates with hot, dry summers.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew conifer and tree records

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in a cool, sheltered, humid site; this is an extremely slow-growing conifer best treated as a long-term collector's specimen.

directions: One of the slowest-growing and longest-lived conifers in the world, this Tasmanian riverbank relic has soft, drooping, scale-like foliage on weeping branchlets and a distinctive resinous fragrance when the foliage or timber is cut. It requires a cool, consistently humid, sheltered site with moist but well-drained acidic soil, mimicking the riverside gorges of western Tasmania where it is naturally found. Growth is measured in inches per decade rather than per year, so it suits patient collectors and conifer gardens rather than gardeners wanting quick cover. Protect young plants from drying wind and scorching sun, and avoid any soil that dries out in summer.

planting.note: Plant in spring in cool, moist, humus-rich soil; this high-altitude Tasmanian conifer tolerates more cold than many rainforest relatives but still dislikes hot, dry summers.

directions: Native to Tasmania's high alpine plateaus, this columnar conifer carries tiny, closely overlapping scale leaves that give its upright branches a smooth, cord-like appearance, quite distinct from the larger, more open foliage of its lowland relative Athrotaxis selaginoides. It is naturally adapted to cold winters and cool summers with reliable moisture, so it does best in climates with mild, humid summers rather than continental heat. Plant in acidic to neutral, moisture-retentive but free-draining soil, and expect very slow growth that eventually forms a dense, narrow, long-lived specimen. It is a collector's conifer best suited to rock gardens, scree beds, or dedicated conifer collections.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew conifer records

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in cool, moist, acidic soil with reliable humidity; this is Australia's only cold-deciduous tree and colors well where summers stay mild.

directions: This Tasmanian alpine endemic is Australia's only winter-deciduous native tree, forming a low, gnarled, often multi-stemmed shrub in exposed subalpine heath and a more upright small tree in sheltered gullies. Its small, crinkled, fan-shaped leaves turn gold, orange, and red before dropping in autumn, giving it genuine four-season appeal in a cool-climate garden. It needs consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil and a cool, humid climate, struggling badly wherever summers are hot and dry. Give it shelter from strong wind and some protection from the hottest midday sun, and treat it as a slow-growing specimen for rock gardens, scree beds, or collections of Southern Hemisphere cool-temperate plants.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew conifer and tree records

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring into sharply drained, gritty soil; this hybrid spreads as a mat and resents wet, heavy ground.

directions: A garden hybrid between the Scottish Highland native Dryas octopetala and the North American Dryas drummondii, this creeping evergreen subshrub forms a dense, woody mat of small, glossy, oak-shaped leaves and holds the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. Its large, creamy-white, slightly nodding flowers open from pale yellow buds from late spring into summer and are followed by distinctive silky, twisted seed heads. It is extremely cold-hardy and wind-tolerant but demands sharp drainage, full sun, and lean, gritty soil to avoid rot, making it well suited to rock gardens, scree beds, troughs, and dry stone walls. Established plants are very drought-tolerant and should never be given rich soil or excess summer water.

planting.note: Divide and replant in spring or early autumn into gritty, humus-rich soil; it roots readily from the trailing rosette offsets.

directions: Native to rocky Highland and upland British habitats, this mat-forming saxifrage produces trailing, moss-like rosettes of narrow, deeply lobed leaves that stay evergreen through winter. In late spring it sends up short, wiry stems topped with small, white, five-petaled flowers held just above the foliage mat. It prefers gritty, well-drained but not dry soil with some organic matter, and tolerates full sun in cool climates or light shade where summers run hot. It is an easy, reliable groundcover for rock gardens, wall crevices, and the edges of raised beds, and spreads readily by rooting where its trailing shoots touch soil.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into a permanently moist, cool spot such as a trough with a drip reservoir or bog-garden edge; it fails quickly if allowed to dry out.

directions: This small rosette-forming saxifrage grows naturally in the wet flushes, streamsides, and dripping rock ledges of the Scottish Highlands, so it needs constantly moist, cool, humus-rich soil to thrive in the garden. Its loose sprays of white, star-shaped flowers appear in summer, each petal marked with two yellow spots near the base and a scatter of tiny red dots, giving the flowers a distinctive jeweled look up close. It resents any drying out at the roots and is best grown in an alpine trough with a constant water supply, a shaded scree by a garden pool, or a cool bog garden rather than an ordinary rock garden. Light shade from the hottest sun and a steady supply of moisture are more important to its success than rich feeding.

planting.note: Sow seed in spring or divide established clumps; set out into sharply drained, gritty soil and avoid rich or waterlogged ground.

directions: A tight, tufted rock-garden perennial from cold, exposed mountain ledges including a handful of Scottish Highland and northern English summits, this little campion forms a low cushion of narrow basal leaves. In late spring and early summer it sends up short stems topped with dense, rounded clusters of small, deep pink to magenta flowers. It is extremely cold-hardy and wind-tolerant but needs sharp drainage and lean, gritty soil, since damp or fertile conditions quickly cause the tight rosettes to rot. Grow it in a scree bed, trough, or raised rock garden in full sun, and avoid winter wet by siting it where water drains away freely.

common_name: Dwarf Bog Rosemary 'Compacta' (Compact Blue-Leaf Bog Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container divisions in spring directly into permanently saturated, strongly acidic peat so the shallow root system never dries out.

directions: 'Compacta' is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit selection of the circumpolar bog shrub Andromeda polifolia, forming a dense, tidy mound far smaller than the straggly wild species. Its narrow, blue-green, rolled-margin leaves are held on compact, closely branched stems, and in mid to late spring it smothers itself in tight clear-pink buds that open to nodding, urn-shaped flowers with a hint of white. Like the species, it demands permanently wet, nutrient-poor, strongly acidic peat and full sun to light shade, making it suitable only for dedicated bog gardens, peat beds, or container bog plantings rather than ordinary garden soil. Its reduced size makes it a favorite for miniature bog gardens and trough plantings where the full-sized species would be too large.

common_name: Bog Rosemary 'Blue Ice' (Silvery-Blue Dwarf Bog Rosemary)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings in spring into constantly saturated, acidic peat; established plants spread slowly by a shallow, fibrous root system.

directions: 'Blue Ice' is a named selection of bog rosemary grown chiefly for its intensely icy, silvery-blue foliage, a more pronounced glaucous tone than the species, set off by small nodding pink bell-shaped flowers typical of the genus in spring. Growth is slow and dense, forming a low, tight dome that rarely exceeds ten inches, making it a popular choice for rock-garden-style bog plantings and troughs where its foliage color reads clearly against moss or gravel mulch. As with all Andromeda polifolia forms, it requires permanently wet, nutrient-poor, strongly acidic peat and cannot be grown successfully in ordinary well-drained garden soil. It is best sited in full sun in cool climates, with light shade recommended where summers are hot, to preserve the strongest blue foliage color.
